sections.body_en:
One of the central questions in the laws of guarding one's life, and in our generation perhaps the main question, is: what is the attitude of halakha to a person who violates the road safety laws? Does a person who drives at excessive speed, or overtakes where there is a marking forbidding it, or does not keep his distance, thereby transgress a Torah prohibition or not?

Since the question is important, and I knew that the true answer might not be pleasant to some of the learners, I did not rely on my own judgement, and I turned to the Chief Rabbi, Rabbi Avraham Shapira shlita, and asked him whether according to halakha there is a prohibition against violating the traffic laws, and if there is a prohibition, how severe it is – whether it is a Torah prohibition or a rabbinic one. And his answer was unequivocal: a person who drives at high speed (of the kind it is customary to punish) or a person who does not obey the other safety laws transgresses a Torah prohibition. This is because the Torah commanded us to guard our lives diligently, and the meaning is not only not to commit suicide, but to keep away from danger and to be careful. And of course the traffic laws were not set arbitrarily in order to annoy drivers; rather, they were set by experts who examined and researched the subject and reached the conclusion that at such a speed, or in overtaking at this place, and the like, there is danger; and so a person who violates these laws transgresses the Torah prohibition.

The basis for the duty to beware of dangerous things we learned from the mitzva of the guardrail, as it is said (Devarim 22:8): "When you build a new house, you shall make a guardrail for your roof, so that you do not bring blood upon your house if anyone falls from it." And the Sages added and explained (Sifrei there) that the Torah's intention in the mitzva of the guardrail is to teach us a general mitzva: that we should beware and guard ourselves against all dangers.

That is, the roof without the guardrail is an example of a dangerous situation, which the Torah commands us to prevent by means of a guardrail. And so is the law regarding all hazards and dangers: we must guard ourselves against them and remove them. And so the Rambam ruled (Laws of the Murderer and Guarding Life 11:4), that any obstacle that involves danger to life, it is a positive mitzva to remove it and to guard against it and to be very, very careful in the matter, as it is said (Devarim 4:9): "Take heed to yourself and guard your soul." And if he did not remove it and left the obstacles that lead to danger, he has neglected a positive mitzva and transgressed "so that you do not bring blood upon your house."

It should be emphasised that one who does not keep the safety laws, even if luck smiled on him and no accident happened to him, nevertheless, by not being careful he has transgressed a Torah prohibition, since the Torah commanded us to be careful. And so the answer of the Chief Rabbi, Rabbi Shapira, is clear: whoever violates the traffic laws, which are intended to prevent danger to life and which were set by experts at the price of precious blood, neglects a Torah mitzva and transgresses "so that you do not bring blood upon your house."

In addition, everyone who drives without care must know that even if he personally has not caused any accident, he is nevertheless to blame for the existence of road accidents. For by his fast and careless driving he has helped create a negative norm, and certainly caused more drivers to follow in his footsteps and try to keep up with his fast pace, and in all likelihood one of them will be hurt.

In addition to the Torah mitzva of guarding one's life, one who violates the safety laws also transgresses the prohibition of violating a communal enactment. For the Knesset that passed these laws was elected by the public, and therefore its enactments have binding force.

This is not the place to explain from a halakhic point of view the force of communal enactments – whether by virtue of "what the beit din declares ownerless is ownerless", or by virtue of "the law of the kingdom is the law" according to most poskim, or by virtue of the definitions of partnership (see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land" 6:1-5). But in any case it is clear that as long as the law does not contradict halakha, it has binding force. Therefore a person who violates the traffic laws, in addition to his carelessness, which involves a Torah prohibition, also transgresses a prohibition in not taking into account the enactments enacted by the public's representatives.

A driver who violates the safety laws in vehicles belonging to the IDF transgresses a further prohibition of theft. For it is clear that the army in no way agrees that its vehicles be driven other than according to the traffic laws and military regulations. Therefore one who drives a military vehicle not according to the law, even if nothing happened, is nevertheless using the vehicle without permission, and transgresses theft. And as is known, theft from the public is more severe than theft from an individual.

And so is the law for every person who drives a vehicle that does not belong to him – for example, those who drive a vehicle belonging to a settlement or a kibbutz, or drivers in a taxi or bus company. For in all likelihood the company insists that its drivers drive according to the law, and if they violate the traffic laws they also transgress the prohibition of using a vehicle without permission.

Sometimes the question arises: what should a person do who is travelling in a bus or a taxi, and the driver is driving at excessive speed, contrary to the law – should he comment to him or not? More than the question is difficult halakhically, it is difficult because of the unpleasantness involved; for from the point of view of halakha it is clear that one should approach the driver and comment to him on his driving not according to the safety rules. For even if there is one percent chance that the driver will listen, it is a mitzva to comment to him (MB 608:3). And the Sages said that whoever is able to protest, and there is a chance that perhaps they will listen to him, and did not protest, is guilty of that same sin (Shabbat 54b). And as long as there is still some chance that the rebuke will help, one must rebuke again, as the Sages said (Bava Metzia 31a): "'You shall surely rebuke' – even a hundred times is implied."

Moreover, even if it is clear that the driver will not respond to us, one should comment to him, because in any case there is a duty to rebuke in order to say the truth. For even if at this moment the rebuke does not help, it will certainly have an influence for the future – and if not on this driver, then on another driver (Rema OḤ 608:2, and MB there).

But one must know that when one rebukes a person, one should try not to insult him, as it is said (Vayikra 19:17): "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him." And the Sages said in the Sifra: "Could it be even if his face changes?" – that is, he is insulted – "Scripture says, 'and not bear sin because of him'"; that is, rebuke him privately and out of love, and then he will not be hurt and not be insulted. Admittedly, if after the required care the driver is insulted, there is no sin at all on the part of the one who rebuked him. On the contrary, the mitzva is to rebuke him even if he becomes angry, and in the view of the Rambam one should rebuke the sinner until he almost wants to strike the one rebuking (Laws of Character Traits 6:7; and see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land" 7:3-5).

A person is obligated to save his fellow who is in danger, as it is said (Vayikra 19:16): "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour." In this mitzva the Torah guides us not to stand aside at a time when another person is in danger. We are forbidden to be indifferent, and we must act with all the means at our disposal to save him. If one sees a person drowning in the sea, for example, one is obligated to jump in and save him. And likewise, if robbers attack a Jew, everyone who sees this is obligated to rise to his aid. And if a person falls into a dangerous illness and does not have the sum required for the medical treatment, each of his friends and acquaintances must give of their money in order to save him. And of course the doctor treating him, too, if he sees that he has no money to pay, is obligated to treat him and heal him free of charge. And one who sees a Jew in danger and did not try to save him has transgressed the prohibition of "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" (SA ḤM 426; and see below 11:1-3 on the definitions of the mitzva).

That is, in addition to the personal mitzva incumbent on each of us to guard his own life from dangers, there is a further mitzva to guard and save the life of another.

And if one must do everything in order to save another person of Israel, all the more so must one be careful not to harm or endanger another person. And this mitzva of "You shall not stand by the blood of your neighbour" too must stand before each and every driver. For the driver must think not only of himself, but also of the others whom he may harm if he does not drive carefully.

This is the place to comment on the custom of many young people who long to get a driving licence and start driving, to feel the sense of freedom and release that a person can feel when he operates a powerful car capable of carrying him great distances at great speed. Despite the challenge and the sense of maturity that accompany getting the licence and driving in the first years, every person who gets behind the wheel must get into the car with fear and trembling, with quaking and sweat, and be very afraid lest he cause, Heaven forbid, a road accident. Therefore there is no place to hurry to get into the car and drive.

sections.title_en: 5. A Kohen Who Ran a Person Over and Killed Him
sections.body_en:
A kohen who ran a person over and killed him is disqualified from raising his hands and blessing Israel with the Priestly Blessing, as is brought in the Talmud, tractate Berakhot (Berakhot 32b): "Rabbi Yoḥanan said: A kohen who killed a person shall not raise his hands, as it is said (Yeshayahu 1:15): 'And when you spread forth your hands I will hide My eyes from you; even when you make many prayers I will not hear; your hands are full of blood.'" That is, when the kohen's hands are not clean of blood, he cannot bless Israel. And there is no difference between one who kills deliberately and one who kills unintentionally; in any case, since in fact he killed, his hands are not clean, and he cannot raise his hands and bless Israel. And if he blessed, his blessing is in vain (Rambam, Laws of Prayer 15:3; SA OḤ 128:35).

And if the kohen returns in complete teshuva for this, in the view of the Shulḥan Arukh (OḤ 128:35), even teshuva does not help, for an accuser cannot become a defender, and a kohen who killed can never again raise his hands and bless Israel. And in the view of the Rema, if he did teshuva he may raise his hands. And what is meant here is not a mere thought of teshuva, but a deep teshuva; that is, the driver who ran someone over should go to a sage who will arrange for him an order of teshuva, which begins with the correction of his deeds and setting up fences in the matter in which he sinned, and continues to taking on fasts and giving abundant tzedaka.

And there is a middle view: a kohen who killed unintentionally and did teshuva may raise his hands, but a kohen who killed deliberately cannot raise his hands even after teshuva (Pri Ḥadash, Eliya Rabba; Bi'ur Halakha 128:35). In practice, a kohen to whom such a grave event happened should go to his rabbi to receive personal instruction on how to conduct himself.

But if there was no negligence at all in his driving – for example, a child suddenly jumped under the wheels of his car, and it was not in his power to prevent running him over – in such a case he is not even considered one who killed unintentionally, but under compulsion, and according to all views, if he does teshuva according to the instruction of a sage, he may afterwards return and raise his hands (Yeḥaveh Da'at 5:16). However, one should not rely in this on the testimony of the driver who ran the person over; rather, upright and wise people are needed to examine the case without partiality, and if it indeed becomes clear that the kohen ran the person over under compulsion, after he does teshuva for the terrible event that happened through him, he may return to raising his hands.

Having dealt with the danger of the roads, it is fitting to learn about the prayer that the Sages instituted for travellers – Tefillat Ha-Derekh, the Traveller's Prayer. In the past the danger of the roads came from robbers, wild beasts or natural hazards. Today the main danger is from road accidents. In any case, the same prayer that the Sages instituted suits all kinds of dangers on the roads.

One should preface that the most protected place for people is their natural surroundings, that is, the home or the town. But when a person is cut off from the town, from his friends and neighbours, and sets out on the road, he is exposed to a certain danger. If he is attacked there will be fewer people who can come to his aid. And if he is hurt, more time will pass until he is taken to hospital. Therefore the Sages instituted Tefillat Ha-Derekh.

When we look at the wording of the prayer, we find that the prayer is said in the plural, and this is not by chance. From a spiritual point of view, being cut off from the community is the root of the danger of the road; therefore one who sets out on the road must associate himself with the community as much as possible, and thereby his prayer will be more readily accepted.

Since we are already standing in prayer before the Creator and asking that the journey pass in peace, we add a request to Hashem that He also make our way successful (Berakhot 29b; 30a). And this is the wording of the prayer: "May it be Your will, Hashem our God and God of our fathers, that You lead us in peace, direct our steps in peace, guide us in peace, and bring us to our desired destination for life, for joy and for peace. Save us from the hand of every enemy and ambush on the way, and from all kinds of calamities that come upon the world. Send blessing upon the work of our hands, and grant us grace, kindness and mercy in Your eyes and in the eyes of all who see us. Hear the voice of our supplications, for You are God who hears prayer and supplication. Blessed are You, Hashem, who hears prayer." And there are certain differences between several versions of Tefillat Ha-Derekh, and all of them are good.

Some asked about the wording of Tefillat Ha-Derekh: why does it not open with "Blessed"? For we have a rule: every blessing that is not adjacent to another, that is, which is said on its own, must open with a blessing, that is, with the words "Blessed are You, Hashem". If so, Tefillat Ha-Derekh, which is said as a single prayer, why does it not open with the words "Blessed"?

And indeed, because of this some were stringent always to attach Tefillat Ha-Derekh to another blessing (Maharam of Rothenburg). And ideally it is good to be stringent, and if another blessing happens to come a person's way when he begins his journey, it is preferable to attach Tefillat Ha-Derekh to it immediately. For example, if he ate an apple and must make the after-blessing, he should first make the after-blessing and then Tefillat Ha-Derekh. But if no blessing happens to come his way, according to most poskim one may say Tefillat Ha-Derekh even without another blessing before it. The reason for this is that in essence Tefillat Ha-Derekh is not a blessing at all but a prayer, and the rules of blessings do not apply to it; therefore it does not open with the words "Blessed are You" etc., and it also need not be adjacent to another (Tosafot Pesaḥim 104b; MB 110:28).

This is proven from the ending of the prayer, which is not the usual ending of a blessing, but only "Blessed are You, Hashem, who hears prayer," without mentioning the words "our God, King of the universe". And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: every blessing that does not contain the Name and Kingship is not a blessing (Berakhot 40b). And since in Tefillat Ha-Derekh one does not say "our God, King of the universe", it is not a blessing but a prayer.

And there is another answer: that Tefillat Ha-Derekh is indeed a blessing – the blessing "who hears prayer" of the Shemoneh Esreh, for at the end we say, "Blessed are You, Hashem, who hears prayer." And if we ask why it does not open with "Blessed", the answer is that since the blessing "who hears prayer" in the Shemoneh Esreh prayer is generally adjacent to the blessings before it, even when it is said separately, as for example in Tefillat Ha-Derekh, the Sages did not change its wording. And there is no need to open it with the words "Blessed" and to mention in it the words "our God, King of the universe", since they were already mentioned in the previous blessings of the Shemoneh Esreh, and there is no need to repeat them again in the blessing "who hears prayer" (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona on Berakhot 2a).

sections.title_en: 8. Over Which Journey One Says It
sections.body_en:
The Sages instituted that Tefillat Ha-Derekh be said for a journey longer than a parsa (Berakhot 30a). A parsa is about four kilometres. And if the journey is shorter, one does not say it. The reason for this is that a journey of less than four kilometres is in all likelihood close to a settled area, and there is no danger in it.

Seemingly there is no difference whether one covers this distance on foot, riding a donkey or travelling in a fast car; the main thing is that if its length is more than a parsa one says Tefillat Ha-Derekh, and if less, one does not say it. However, some of the poskim held that the measure of a parsa is meant to give us a measure of time: that if the journey takes more than seventy-two minutes, which is the time it takes an average person to walk four kilometres on an unpaved road, one must say Tefillat Ha-Derekh; but if the journey takes less than seventy-two minutes, since the danger does not last long, one does not say Tefillat Ha-Derekh. According to this, today a person who travels from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem would not say Tefillat Ha-Derekh, because the time it takes to travel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem is less than seventy-two minutes (see Responsa Zikhron Yehuda OḤ 42).

But in the view of most poskim, the intention of the Sages when they said a parsa is to set the length of the journey over which one must say Tefillat Ha-Derekh. For the longer the journey, the further it goes from settled areas, and so its dangers increase. But time has no significance; it is a fact that in the time of the Sages too people rode horses and would cover four kilometres in less than ten minutes, and nevertheless the Sages did not distinguish between one walking and one riding, and established that for a journey of a parsa one says Tefillat Ha-Derekh. According to this, in our time too, when there are fast cars, one measures the length of the journey, and if it is more than a parsa one is obligated to say Tefillat Ha-Derekh. And so ruled the author of the Mishna Berura (MB 110:30), and this is the halakha, because the great majority of poskim ruled so ("Ahalekh Ba-Amitekha" p. 101). And especially today, when road accidents constitute one of the main dangers to human life. It should be added that some hold that Tefillat Ha-Derekh is not a blessing, and therefore there is no concern in it of the prohibition of a blessing in vain.

And one who travels a great deal within the city would do well to say Tefillat Ha-Derekh without mentioning Hashem's Name at its end, that is, he should end the prayer "Blessed are You, who hears prayer." And one should not say Tefillat Ha-Derekh in the city with Hashem's Name, because the Sages instituted the prayer for one travelling outside the city, and it is not in our power to change their enactment. But to say the prayer without Hashem's Name is certainly right. For although inter-city travel is more dangerous, nevertheless travel within the city too involves danger, and it is fitting to pray about it.

Tefillat Ha-Derekh should be said after we have already begun the journey – not inside the city itself, but immediately after leaving the city. Admittedly, in the view of the Taz one must say it as soon as one begins the journey, even while still inside the city. But according to most poskim one must say it specifically after leaving the city (MB 110:29).

And one should not wait; rather, one must say it immediately on leaving the city. And if he forgot to say it when leaving the city, if about four kilometres still remain to his destination, he can still say it; but for less than that he should not conclude with "Blessed" (SA OḤ 110:7).

And a person who makes several journeys in a day need say Tefillat Ha-Derekh only the first time, and intend in his request all the journeys he will make that day. But if he planned only one journey, and afterwards changed his mind and decided to travel again, then he must say it a second time (SA OḤ 110:5).

Ideally, while saying Tefillat Ha-Derekh one should stop walking, and stand or sit. Seemingly the law is the same when travelling by car: if the driver must say Tefillat Ha-Derekh, it would seemingly be preferable for him to park at the side of the road and say Tefillat Ha-Derekh. And if the driver has already said Tefillat Ha-Derekh that day and only the other passengers need to say Tefillat Ha-Derekh, there is no need to park the vehicle, because the travel does not disturb their concentration (SA OḤ 110:4, MB 23).

However, in practice it seems that even when the driver must say Tefillat Ha-Derekh one should not be particular about this, because parking at the side of the road involves a certain degree of danger, and there is a concern that being particular about it will over time cause risk to life. Therefore it is better that the driver always get used to saying Tefillat Ha-Derekh while driving.

sections.title_en: 10. Tefillat Ha-Derekh on the Roads of Judea, Samaria and Gaza
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, because of the danger on the roads the Sages instituted the saying of Tefillat Ha-Derekh. However, from the Babylonian Talmud (Berakhot 31a) it is implied that if the journey is shorter than a parsa (about four kilometres), there is no danger in it, and therefore one should not say Tefillat Ha-Derekh over it. But this was challenged from the words of the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot 4:4), which establishes that all roads are presumed dangerous, and the implication is that there is no difference between a journey of more than a parsa and a journey of less than a parsa. And Rabbeinu Yona answered in his commentary on tractate Berakhot (Berakhot 20b) that the Babylonian Talmud speaks of an ordinary road, which, if its length is less than a parsa, has no danger, and therefore one should not say Tefillat Ha-Derekh on it; whereas the Yerushalmi speaks of a more dangerous road, and therefore even for a journey of less than a parsa one should say Tefillat Ha-Derekh. And so it was ruled in halakha: if the road is presumed dangerous, even if it is shorter than a parsa, one should say Tefillat Ha-Derekh on it (MB 110:30).

If so, on those roads in Judea, Samaria and Gaza that are considered dangerous because of attacks by Arabs who throw stones, and sometimes even throw firebombs or shoot, one should say Tefillat Ha-Derekh even for a journey of less than a parsa. And although in the long term the danger of road accidents is more severe than the danger of attacks – for it is a fact that more people from the settlements are hurt in road accidents than by terrorist activity – nevertheless the danger of road accidents is the danger of an ordinary road, on which one says Tefillat Ha-Derekh only if one travels more than four kilometres. But in Judea, Samaria and Gaza a further danger is added that is not common on ordinary roads, and therefore one should say Tefillat Ha-Derekh even for a journey of one kilometre. And may it be His will that all our enemies and the foes of our lives come to an end, and that Israel dwell securely in all the expanses of its land.
